title: Responses to the Munich Agreement, 1938
stem:
The following sources are original practice texts written in the style of the period.

Source A: Extract from a fictional speech by a British Conservative MP in the House of Commons, October 1938.
"We are told that peace has been saved. Perhaps for a season it has. But we have bought it by handing over the fortresses of a friendly democracy to a man who has broken every promise he has made. The Czechs were not even asked. I fear we have not satisfied an appetite; we have fed it."

Source B: Extract from a fictional editorial in a British regional newspaper, 1 October 1938.
"The Prime Minister has flown three times to Germany to spare this country a war for which it is not ready and which few here wish to fight over a quarrel in central Europe. The German-speaking people of the Sudetenland have long asked to join their kinsmen. Their wish is granted, and our sons stay at home."

Source C: Extract from a fictional secondary work by a historian, 2015.
"Chamberlain's policy at Munich must be judged against Britain's weakness in 1938: an air force still re-equipping, Dominions reluctant to fight and a public that remembered the Somme. Yet the agreement also revealed his misreading of Hitler, whom he treated as a statesman with limited aims. The occupation of Prague six months later exposed that misjudgement."

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: According to Source B, why did the Prime Minister agree to the transfer of the Sudetenland?
markscheme: Britain was not ready for war
few people in Britain wanted to fight over a central European quarrel
the Sudeten Germans had long wished to join Germany / self-determination
the agreement kept British soldiers at home / avoided casualties
parts.notes: Award 1 mark per relevant point, up to 3.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: What is the message of Source A?
markscheme: the agreement only buys a temporary peace
Hitler cannot be trusted / has broken promises
Czechoslovakia was betrayed and excluded
appeasement will encourage further German demands ('fed' his appetite)
parts.notes: Award 1 mark per point, up to 2.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for a historian studying the reasons for the Munich Agreement.
markscheme: Value (origin): written by a historian in 2015 with hindsight and access to archives and later scholarship
Value (purpose): intended to explain and assess Chamberlain's policy, so it weighs several factors
Value (content): identifies military weakness, Dominion reluctance and public opinion as constraints, and Chamberlain's misjudgement of Hitler
Limitation (origin/purpose): a short extract may reflect one historian's interpretation / hindsight may lead to judging Chamberlain by what happened later
Limitation (content): does not consider French policy or Soviet exclusion / gives no detail on Hitler's aims
parts.notes: Do not award marks for generic comments ('it is secondary so it is reliable'). Maximum 3 if only value or only limitations are addressed.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Compare and contrast what Sources A and B reveal about British attitudes to the Munich Agreement.
markscheme: Similarity: both accept that the agreement avoided (or postponed) war
Similarity: both refer to the transfer of Czechoslovak territory to Germany
Difference: A condemns the agreement; B praises the Prime Minister
Difference: A stresses betrayal of Czechoslovakia ('not even asked'); B stresses the Sudeten Germans' right to join Germany
Difference: A sees Hitler as untrustworthy and expects more demands; B treats the issue as a settled local quarrel
Difference: A sees peace as temporary ('for a season'); B sees it as protecting British lives now
parts.notes: Award up to 6 marks for at least one similarity and several differences presented as linked comparisons. End-on descriptions of each source: maximum 3.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Using the sources and your own knowledge, evaluate the reasons why Britain and France pursued appeasement in 1938.
markscheme: Focused argument that weighs several reasons and reaches a judgement
Military unpreparedness: RAF re-equipping, fear of bombing of cities (Source C)
Public opinion and memory of the First World War / pacifism (Sources B, C)
Belief that Versailles was harsh and German grievances, including self-determination of the Sudeten Germans, were partly justified (Source B)
Dominion reluctance to fight; economic weakness after the Depression; need to protect the empire
French dependence on Britain and reluctance to act alone, despite its alliance with Czechoslovakia
Distrust of the USSR / fear of communism, excluding Stalin from Munich
Chamberlain's personal belief that Hitler had limited aims / misjudgement of Hitler (Sources A, C)
Historiography: 'guilty men' versus revisionist view of constraints (e.g. R.A.C. Parker on alternatives)
Explicit use of sources integrated with own knowledge
parts.notes: Paper 1 Question 4 is marked with markbands: the top band (7–9) needs a focused, well-structured response integrating sources AND accurate own knowledge with a clear judgement.
